title: MLflow, experiments and reproducibility
summary: A model's number is only as good as the record behind it: what a run holds, when two runs compare, when a rerun reproduces, what a packaged model promises, and how a version earns an alias.
outcomes: Name what an MLflow run records (parameters, metrics, tags, datasets, artifacts, a logged model) and where each part is stored.
Decide whether two runs are comparable from their dataset digests and differing parameters, and read a sorted table against its baselines.
Rerun a run from its record, recognize a run that cannot be reproduced, and refuse a rerun on changed data or a different library version.
Read a logged model's flavors, signature and environment, and predict which input drift MLflow rejects and which a contract must catch.
Promote a registered version by moving an alias only after a versioned contract's evidence gate and thresholds pass, and separate open-source duties from those of models in Unity Catalog.
startingAssumptions: The machine-learning foundations module has covered targets, prediction moments, baselines, leakage and deployment-shaped splits.
Python and pandas can be read; no prior MLflow experience is assumed.
editorialRationale: MLflow is usually taught as an API tour, which leaves learners able to log runs they cannot defend. The module instead follows one executed experiment: it defines the record, shows what a dataset digest does and does not prove, then uses the record to compare runs, expose a superior-looking run that cannot be rerun and reproduce a clean one exactly. Packaging, signatures and environments come next as the model's promises, and the registry closes the loop with promotion by evidence. Version-specific behaviour is labelled as observed in the lab, and the Databricks-managed column is kept separate from what was executed.

claims.description: An experiment groups runs; a run records parameters, metrics with an optional step history, tags and artifacts; a backend store keeps run metadata and an artifact store keeps files.

mlflow.data builds a dataset with a name, an automatically computed digest, a source and optional schema and profile; mlflow.log_input attaches it to a run with a context such as training or evaluation.
A logged MLflow model is a directory with an MLmodel file listing its flavors; python_function is the generic interface built-in flavors include.

Signature enforcement runs when a model is loaded as python_function or used by MLflow deployment tools, not with native-flavor loading; missing required inputs raise and only lossless type conversions are made.
Logging a model writes requirements.txt, python_env.yaml and conda.yaml describing the environment that loads it; extra requirements can be added at logging time.
A registered model holds numbered versions with lineage to their runs; aliases are mutable references to one version, a version can hold several aliases, and tags annotate versions.

In MLflow 3 a logged model is a first-class entity with a model ID, referenced as models:/<model_id>, to which metrics can be linked.
The file-based tracking backend is superseded by database backends; mlflow migrate-filestore (MLflow 3.10 or later) moves its metadata to SQLite and leaves artifacts in place.
Databricks-managed MLflow hosts tracking in the workspace, where experiments carry permission levels, and registers models in Unity Catalog, the default registry with MLflow 3.

concepts.definition: A named container that groups related runs so they can be searched and compared together.
concepts.example: cinderline-oven-fault-warning holds the baselines, the clean runs, the leaks and the hero.

concepts.definition: One execution of training or evaluation code, recorded with its parameters, metrics, tags, datasets and artifacts.
concepts.example: time-split-C-1 records C=1.0, seed 20260923, recall 0.8333 and its model.

concepts.definition: An input value chosen before a run, stored as text and fixed once logged.
concepts.example: C is stored as the text 1.0; logging C=0.5 later is refused.

concepts.definition: A numeric result measured by a run, optionally logged at several steps with the latest shown.
concepts.example: recall 0.8333 and warnings_per_day 1.8889 for time-split-C-1.

concepts.definition: A file a run writes to the artifact store, such as a report, a plot or a model directory.
concepts.example: The clean run's split report, checks/split_report.json, and its confusion matrix.

concepts.definition: A short hash MLflow computes from a logged dataset's content that identifies which rows a run saw.
concepts.example: 4950f73b for days 1 to 84; 3f06bea0 for the random split's rows.

concepts.definition: A column recorded after the prediction moment, so a model using it cannot run when the prediction is needed.
concepts.example: repair_minutes, written by the technician after the fault it would predict.

concepts.definition: Two runs trained on the same rows that differ in exactly one deliberate parameter.
concepts.example: time-split-C-1 and time-split-C-0.01 share digest 4950f73b and differ only in C.

concepts.definition: A simple predictor logged as a run in the same experiment so that every model is read against it.
concepts.example: never-warn at accuracy 0.9375 and the temperature rule at recall 0.6667.

concepts.definition: A run whose logged parameters, training data and environment let a rerun return the same numbers.
concepts.example: The clean rerun of time-split-C-1 returned digest 4950f73b and identical metrics.

concepts.definition: A named way to load a logged model, listed in its MLmodel file, such as python_function or sklearn.
concepts.example: The lab's model lists python_function and sklearn, saved as model.skops.

concepts.definition: The named, typed inputs and outputs recorded with a model and enforced when it is loaded as python_function.
concepts.example: Six required double inputs and fault_next_24h as a long output.

concepts.definition: A versioned document stating a model's inputs, output, thresholds and the evidence a run must carry.
concepts.example: Contract 1.0.0: six doubles, recall at least 0.75, at most 2.0 warnings a day.

concepts.definition: The Python version and pinned packages written beside a logged model so it can be loaded again.
concepts.example: requirements.txt pins mlflow 3.16.1 and scikit-learn 1.9.1.

concepts.definition: A numbered registration of a logged model under a registered model's name; its model files and source run do not change, though its tags can.
concepts.example: cinderline-oven-fault version 1 came from time-split-C-1.

concepts.definition: A mutable name that points at exactly one version of a registered model.
concepts.example: models:/cinderline-oven-fault@candidate loads version 1 after the rollback.

concepts.definition: Moving an alias to a version only after its run passes a contract's evidence gate and then its thresholds.
concepts.example: Only time-split-C-1 passed both gates and became the candidate.

concepts.definition: Databricks' model registry, where models have catalog.schema.model names, catalog privileges, aliases and no stages.
concepts.example: cinderline_ml.maintenance.oven_fault with the alias candidate.

concepts.definition: Moving a self-hosted MLflow file-based backend's metadata into a database backend.
concepts.example: mlflow migrate-filestore copies ./mlruns metadata into SQLite.

concepts.definition: MLflow 3's first-class record of a logged model, with its own ID, artifacts and linked metrics.
concepts.example: models:/m-<id> loads the model that time-split-C-1 logged, before any registration.

concepts.definition: The Unity Catalog grants that control creating, versioning, aliasing and loading a registered model.
concepts.example: CREATE MODEL on the schema to create; EXECUTE to load for inference.

concepts.definition: The permission levels that decide who can read, log to or manage a Databricks MLflow experiment.
concepts.example: A reviewer is given CAN READ on the workspace experiment holding the oven runs.

questions.prompt: After an outage only the tracking backend database is restored; the artifact store for time-split-C-1 is gone. What can a reviewer still read?

options.text: Parameters, metrics and dataset references, but no model or reports.
options.rationale: Parameters, metrics, tags and dataset metadata live in the backend store; the model and report files lived in the artifact store.

options.text: Its model directory, because the MLmodel file is stored with the run's metadata.
options.rationale: MLmodel is a file inside the model directory in the artifact store, so it went with the artifact store.

options.text: Its split report, because check results are logged as run parameters.
options.rationale: The split report was logged as a JSON artifact; only its conclusion is implied by the split parameter.

options.text: Nothing at all, because MLflow stores each run as a single file.
options.rationale: A run is split across two stores; the backend part survives on its own and still describes what was chosen and measured.

questions.prompt: A notebook cell that logged C=1.0 into the active run is edited to C=0.5 and executed again in the same run. What does MLflow 3.16.1 do?

options.text: It silently replaces the stored 1.0 with 0.5 and keeps no trace of the old value.
options.rationale: Silent replacement would let the record drift away from the model that was trained; MLflow refuses it.

options.text: It keeps 1.0 and 0.5 as a step history, the way it treats a metric.
options.rationale: Only metrics have step histories; parameters hold one value.

options.text: It logs the new value under a second key named C_1.
options.rationale: MLflow never renames keys; the call either matches the stored value or fails.

options.text: It raises an MlflowException: a logged parameter cannot change.
options.rationale: Observed in the lab: the record keeps the first value, and a different choice needs a new run.

questions.prompt: With MLflow 3.16.1, a 50,000-row pandas training frame is logged, then one value in row 30,000 is corrected and the frame is logged again. Row count and columns are unchanged. What happens to the digest?

options.text: MLflow refuses to log a dataset under the same name a second time.
options.rationale: The same dataset can be logged to many runs; each run references it with its own context.

options.text: It stays the same; rows beyond the first 10,000 are not hashed.
options.rationale: Observed in the lab and in the installed code: a change beyond row 10,000 that keeps the shape leaves the digest unchanged.

options.text: It changes, because MLflow hashes every row of the frame on each log_input call.
options.rationale: Only the first 10,000 rows enter the hash in this version; the rest are represented by the row count alone.

options.text: It changes, because the logging timestamp is folded into the digest.
options.rationale: The digest depends on content, row count and column names; timestamps and the source text are not part of it.

questions.prompt: Which pair of the lab's runs lets you attribute its metric difference to a single cause?

options.text: time-split-C-1 and time-split-leaky: same digest, only features differ.
options.rationale: Same rows and one changed parameter isolate the post-event column; accuracy moves from 0.8056 to 1.0 because of it alone.

options.text: time-split-C-1 and random-split-seeded: both use seed 20260923.
options.rationale: A shared seed is not enough: the rows differ (3f06bea0 against 4950f73b) and three parameters change.

options.text: time-split-C-1 and hero: both are logistic regressions.
options.rationale: The hero logged no dataset and eight parameters differ, so nothing about the difference can be attributed.

options.text: hero and hero-again: their records are identical, so the difference is noise.
options.rationale: Identical records with different results mean the cause is unrecorded, the hidden split; that is not a comparison, it is a reproducibility failure.

questions.prompt: In the oven experiment, why does never-warn rank above every honest model when runs are sorted by accuracy?

options.text: Accuracy gives extra weight to the rows where a model issues no warning.
options.rationale: Accuracy counts correct predictions of both classes; never-warn makes no warnings and is wrong only on the 18 faults.

options.text: search_runs always places runs logged as baselines at the top of the table.
options.rationale: search_runs orders by the requested column only; never-warn is third because of its accuracy value.

options.text: Faults are 18 of 288 test rows, so 'no fault' is right 270 times.
options.rationale: Accuracy counts the majority class: 270/288 = 0.9375 with recall 0, which is why the contract reads recall, precision and warnings a day.

options.text: never-warn reads the repair record, which is written after each fault.
options.rationale: never-warn reads nothing at all; its score comes entirely from the class balance.

questions.prompt: The hero and hero-again runs have identical records but different confusion matrices. What does that establish?

options.text: The leak disappeared in the second execution, so its score came from real features.
options.rationale: Both executions read repair_minutes and both score 1.0; only the test population changed.

options.text: The result depends on something the record does not hold.
options.rationale: Identical records with different numbers locate the cause outside the record: here the unseeded random split.

options.text: The model is unstable and would need more training data to converge on one result.
options.rationale: Both executions score perfectly on their own rows; the difference is which rows were tested, not the model's stability.

options.text: MLflow dropped part of the second run's record while writing the file store.
options.rationale: Nothing was lost: the code logged only one parameter both times.

questions.prompt: A rerun of time-split-C-1 on a refreshed extract returns recall 0.81 and a new training digest; the recorded and installed library versions match. How should the result be described?

options.text: A failed reproduction, which shows that the original run's recall was wrong.
options.rationale: A reproduction needs the same rows; with new rows the original claim was never retested.

options.text: A successful reproduction, because 0.81 is within a normal tolerance of 0.8333.
options.rationale: There is no tolerance for changed data: the comparison is between different experiments.

options.text: Evidence that the scikit-learn version changed between the two executions.
options.rationale: The versions match; the digest identifies the data as the thing that changed.

options.text: A new experiment on changed data; it neither confirms nor refutes the original.
options.rationale: The digest shows the rows changed, so the metric difference cannot be attributed to the code or the record.

questions.prompt: A batch job loads the promoted model with mlflow.sklearn.load_model and calls predict on a frame whose humidity column was renamed. What does MLflow's signature enforcement do in this call?

options.text: It renames the column back to humidity_pct using the signature's column list.
options.rationale: Enforcement never repairs inputs; at most it converts types losslessly or refuses.

options.text: It casts every column to double as the signature says, then calls the pipeline.
options.rationale: Only the python_function path applies the signature's types, and only for lossless conversions.

options.text: Nothing; native-flavor loading skips signature enforcement.
options.rationale: Documented: native-flavor loading does not enforce the signature. Any error that follows comes from scikit-learn's own feature-name check, not from MLflow.

options.text: It raises Model is missing inputs ['humidity_pct'] before the pipeline runs.
options.rationale: That message comes from python_function enforcement; the native flavor bypasses it.

questions.prompt: For this signature, which change to a request does MLflow 3.16.1's pyfunc enforcement let through without an error?

options.text: Dropping humidity_pct from the request entirely.
options.rationale: A missing required input raises; the documented rule applies to every required column.

options.text: Adding repair_minutes as a seventh column.
options.rationale: Observed: an input the signature does not name is ignored with a warning, which is why the contract checks a candidate's signature for unexpected inputs and a request needs its own check.

options.text: Renaming humidity_pct to humidity while keeping the same values.
options.rationale: The required input humidity_pct is then missing, and enforcement raises before the model runs.

options.text: Sending door_cycles as int64 values instead of doubles.
options.rationale: int64 to double is not a lossless conversion, so enforcement raises.

questions.prompt: After the rollback, what does models:/cinderline-oven-fault@candidate load, and what happened to version 2?

options.text: Version 1, and the rollback deleted version 2 from the registry.
options.rationale: Rollback moved a pointer; deleting a version is a separate, deliberate action.

options.text: Nothing, until one of the versions is moved to the Production stage.
options.rationale: Aliases replace stages here; models in Unity Catalog do not support stages at all.

options.text: Version 1; version 2 still exists, unchanged, with no alias.
options.rationale: The alias names one version at a time, and moving it never deletes or edits a version.

options.text: Version 2, because the newest registered version always wins.
options.rationale: An alias is explicit; the newest version is loaded only if the alias points at it.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague argues that the leaky run is trustworthy because its record is complete and a rerun reproduces it exactly. Explain what is wrong with the argument and what evidence would settle it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Completeness and reproducibility show that the run can be traced and repeated, not that its inputs were valid. The leaky run reads repair_minutes, which the data dictionary dates after the fault it predicts, so at 09:00 the model could not run; its accuracy 1.0 is a faithful record of an invalid experiment. The evidence that settles it is availability, not provenance: the dictionary entry for each feature, the leakage report logged as an artifact, and a comparison with the same run minus that column, which drops to accuracy 0.8056.
selfQuestions.reasoning: It separates provenance from validity and names the check that decides validity; pointing to the time-split comparison or the evidence gate's post-event rule are equally acceptable ways to finish the argument.

selfQuestions.prompt: The registered model was logged with scikit-learn 1.9.1. The image the platform team builds for batch scoring pins scikit-learn 1.8.0. What do you check, and what do you decide, before the model is loaded there?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Read the model's requirements.txt and MLmodel: they pin scikit-learn 1.9.1 and record the flavor's sklearn_version. A 1.8.0 image is a different environment, so loading may fail or, worse, succeed with different numerics. Decide not to load it there as is: either rebuild the image from the model's requirements.txt or python_env.yaml, or retrain and re-evaluate the model on 1.8.0 as a new run and new version. Record the choice beside the model version.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The environment files are part of the model's promise; a mismatch is resolved by matching the environment or by producing new evidence, never by assuming equivalence. Pinning the image to the model's file is the cheaper usual answer.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the decision entry for time-split-C-0.01, explain why its better recall does not rescue it, and say what would have to happen for a run like it to pass.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: time-split-C-0.01: reject at the thresholds gate; precision_below_min (0.1868 against 0.2) and warnings_above_cap (2.53 a day against 2.0). Its recall of 0.9444 is better, but the round holds two ovens, so 2.53 warnings a day cannot be inspected and a fifth of warnings being real is the owner's floor. Only a changed decision could change the outcome: the maintenance lead agrees a larger round or a lower floor, the contract becomes a new version, and the runs are evaluated again under it.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Thresholds come from the decision's capacity and costs, set before evaluation; moving them after seeing a result is tuning on the test period. Proposing a different threshold on predicted probabilities is also acceptable if it is chosen on validation days before day 85 and confirmed on a period after day 120; re-tuning it on days 85 to 120 would turn the test into development data.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline moves the lab's workflow to a Databricks workspace with Unity Catalog. List what changes in the code, what responsibilities move to the platform, and two that stay with the team.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Code: drop the temporary file store and MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE; log to a workspace experiment; register under a three-level name such as cinderline_ml.maintenance.oven_fault, with databricks-uc as the registry (the default with MLflow 3); keep aliases and tags, never stages. Moving to the platform: hosting the tracking server and stores, experiment permissions, and governance of the model through Unity Catalog privileges such as CREATE MODEL and EXECUTE. Staying with the team: which run earns the alias under the versioned contract, and checking that the logged data was valid and available at 09:00.
selfQuestions.reasoning: It separates operational duties the platform can host from judgements no platform makes, and keeps the registry mechanics (aliases, tags, no stages) consistent across both. Naming entitlement, region and catalog ownership as things to confirm first is also a good answer.

beats.title: A run is the record behind one number
beats.outcome: Name what an MLflow run records and which store keeps each part.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-mlflow-experiment-concept|experiment]] groups [[dbxfe-mlflow-run-concept|runs]], and a run is one execution of training or evaluation code. It records the parameters you chose, the metrics you measured, tags, the datasets it read and the [[dbxfe-mlflow-artifact-concept|artifacts]] it wrote, including a logged model. Notice in the first state that each number a report quotes traces to one of these nodes. In the second, metadata sits in a backend store and files in an artifact store, so losing either one breaks the record in a different way.

handbook.markdown:
A run is opened with `mlflow.start_run()` inside an experiment and closed when the block ends. Everything logged in between belongs to it:

```python
with mlflow.start_run(experiment_id=exp, run_name="time-split-C-1") as run:
    mlflow.log_params({"model": "logistic_regression", "C": 1.0, "seed": 20260923,
                       "split": "time", "train_through_day": 84, "features": ",".join(FEATURES)})
    mlflow.log_input(train_ds, context="training")
    mlflow.log_dict(split_report, "checks/split_report.json")
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", signature=sig, input_example=X.head(3))
    mlflow.log_metrics(metrics, model_id=info.model_id)
```

In the lab's file store the record is visible on disk, which makes the two stores concrete:

```text
tracking/<experiment_id>/<run_id>/meta.yaml         run name, status, start and end time, artifact URI
tracking/<experiment_id>/<run_id>/params/C          the text 1.0
tracking/<experiment_id>/<run_id>/metrics/recall    "<timestamp> <value> <step>" per logged value
tracking/<experiment_id>/<run_id>/inputs/<id>/      dataset references and their context
tracking/<experiment_id>/<run_id>/artifacts/checks/ split and leakage reports
tracking/<experiment_id>/models/<model_id>/artifacts/  MLmodel, model.skops, requirements.txt, ...
```

In MLflow 3 the logged model is its own entity with an ID; metrics logged with `model_id=` attach to it as well as to the run, and the run lists it among its outputs. A database backend keeps the same metadata in tables and an object store keeps the files; the split is the same.

What to inspect when a number is questioned: the run's parameters (what was chosen), its dataset inputs (which rows), its artifacts (the checks that were run) and its model (what was saved). What the record cannot tell you is whether any of it was right; later beats deal with that. Nothing here needs a server: the lab points `mlflow.set_tracking_uri()` at a temporary directory and deletes it afterwards.

beats.recap: A run holds params, metrics, tags, datasets, artifacts and a model, split across a backend and an artifact store.

beats.title: Parameters are written once; metrics are measured
beats.outcome: Predict how MLflow treats a changed parameter and a repeated metric.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-mlflow-param-concept|parameter]] is a choice made before the run, stored as text: C becomes "1.0". A [[dbxfe-mlflow-metric-concept|metric]] is a number the run measured, and it can be logged at several steps, with the latest shown in the run. Notice in the second state that logging C=0.5 into a run that recorded C=1.0 is refused while repeating 1.0 is accepted. The record cannot be edited into agreement with a result; a new choice is a new run.

handbook.markdown:
Parameters are key-value pairs whose values are stored as strings. `mlflow.log_params({"C": 1.0, "seed": 20260923})` stores `"1.0"` and `"20260923"`; a rerun must parse them back (`float(params["C"])`, `int(params["seed"])`), which is one reason to log exactly the values the code reads rather than a description of them. Log the seed and the split's own parameter (`train_through_day=84`, or `train_fraction=0.7` for a random split): without them the rows cannot be recreated.

Immutability was observed directly in the lab:

```python
client.log_param(run_id, "C", 0.5)
# MlflowException: Changing param values is not allowed. Param with key='C' was already
# logged with value='1.0' ...
```

Repeating the identical value is accepted, so idempotent logging code is safe. Metrics are numbers with a timestamp and a step; `mlflow.log_metric("loss", 0.4, step=1)` appends to the history, `run.data.metrics` shows the latest value and `MlflowClient().get_metric_history(run_id, "loss")` returns every step. The lab logs its evaluation metrics once, after training; a training loop would log a loss per epoch.

Two small disciplines pay off later. Do not log a metric that is undefined: precision with no warnings has no value, and a logged zero would be a claim, so the lab omits it for never-warn. And log counts (tp, fp, fn, tn) beside the rates, because rates hide the denominator: recall 0.8333 is 15 of 18 faults.

When a parameter really must change, start a new run with its own name. That also produces what later comparisons need: two runs that differ in exactly the parameter you changed.

beats.recap: Parameters are fixed text choices; metrics are measured numbers with a history.

beats.title: A dataset digest pins which rows a run saw
beats.outcome: Log training and evaluation datasets and use their digests to tell same rows from different rows.
beats.explanation: `mlflow.log_input()` attaches a dataset with a name, source, schema, profile and [[dbxfe-mlflow-digest-concept|digest]], plus a context such as training or evaluation. Log the rows, not only the model's columns: then runs with different feature lists still share a digest. Notice in the first state that C = 1, C = 0.01 and the leaky run share 4950f73b while the random split and the second plant differ. The second state shows the limit: in MLflow 3.16.1 the pandas digest reads at most the first 10,000 rows.

samajh.text: Library mein kitaabon ka ek bada dher aata hai. Librarian poori ginti likhta hai aur sirf upar ki pehli sau kitaabon ke naam note karta hai. Kal agar neeche ki koi kitaab badal di jaaye aur ginti wahi rahe, toh note bilkul wahi rahega. Aur note kabhi yeh nahi batata ki kitaabein sahi hain ya galat; woh bas yeh batata hai ki kaunsa dher tha.
samajh.mapping: The note is the digest: the count is the row count, the noted titles are the first 10,000 rows, and the note identifies the batch without judging its content.
samajh.boundary: A digest is a hash of the rows it reads, not a list of titles; any change among those rows changes it completely, and it never samples at random.

handbook.markdown:
The dataset API wraps the rows a run saw and records their identity without copying them into the store:

```python
train_ds = mlflow.data.from_pandas(train, source="fixtures/oven_days.csv",
                                   name="oven-days-train", targets="fault_next_24h")
mlflow.log_input(train_ds, context="training")
mlflow.log_input(test_ds, context="evaluation")
print(train_ds.digest)   # 4950f73b for days 1-84 of the lab fixture
```

The digest is what makes comparisons checkable: two runs with the same training digest trained on the same rows. That only works if the logged frame is the rows, not the model's column selection. The lab logs every column of the training rows and records the model's columns in the `features` parameter, so a feature ablation keeps its digest.

How the digest is computed matters. Reading the installed MLflow 3.16.1 code and testing it in the lab: the pandas digest hashes the first 10,000 rows (string and numeric columns), the total row count and the column names, and it ignores the source text. So:

- a change inside the first 10,000 rows, a changed row count or a renamed column gives a new digest;
- a changed value after row 10,000, with the same shape, gives the same digest;
- the same frame logged with a different `source` gives the same digest.

For small tables the digest is a strong identity. For large ones, treat it as a fingerprint and record something exact beside it: a table version, a snapshot identifier or a full-file checksum, as a parameter or tag. The digest, in either case, says which data; it says nothing about whether the data was right. That is the next beat.

beats.recap: Log the rows, not the columns; a digest identifies them, within its sampling limit.

beats.title: A complete record can describe an invalid experiment
beats.outcome: Explain why a fully logged run still needs availability and split checks before its metrics mean anything.
beats.explanation: The leaky run logged everything: seed, time split, datasets, signature and artifacts. It also used repair_minutes, a [[dbxfe-mlflow-leak-concept|post-event feature]] the technician writes after the fault it predicts, and scored 1.0. Notice on the timeline that the column exists only at 16:00, hours after the 09:00 prediction. MLflow faithfully recorded it; it cannot know when a column becomes available. A logged run does not certify data quality: that takes separate checks, such as the availability dictionary and the split report, whose outputs the run keeps as artifacts.

handbook.markdown:
Provenance and validity are different properties. MLflow gives provenance: which code parameters, which rows, which files, which model. It has no notion of when a column became available, whether a label was defined honestly, whether rows were duplicated, or whether the test period resembles the future. Those are properties of the data and the design, and they need their own checks.

The lab runs two checks before training and logs both reports as artifacts:

```python
leakage = leakage_report(features)      # reads fixtures/data_dictionary.json
# {"flagged": [{"feature": "repair_minutes", "reason": "recorded_after_prediction",
#               "available_at": "after the fault, same day"}], "ok": false}
split = split_report(train, test)       # time-ordered only if max(train day) < min(test day)
mlflow.log_dict(leakage, "checks/leakage_report.json")
mlflow.log_dict(split, "checks/split_report.json")
```

The leakage check reads the dictionary's `available_at`, never a correlation: a column that predicts the label perfectly is a warning sign, not evidence of skill. The leaky run's report says `ok: false`, and the run was logged anyway, which is exactly the situation a reviewer meets: a complete record whose own artifacts say the experiment is invalid.

The same controlled comparison that isolates a parameter isolates the leak: time-split-C-1 and time-split-leaky share rows and differ only in `features`, and accuracy moves from 0.8056 to 1.0. Scikit-learn's pitfalls guide names the mechanism: information unavailable at prediction time produces overly optimistic estimates, and preprocessing must be learnt from training data only.

What to ask of any run before its metrics: does each feature exist at the prediction moment, is the test period later than the training period, is the label defined the same way in both, and are the check reports attached? A run that reproduces exactly can still fail every one of these.

beats.recap: Provenance is not validity: a complete, reproducible record can hold a leak.

beats.title: Two runs compare only when one thing changed
beats.outcome: Decide whether two runs are comparable from their digests and their differing parameters.
beats.explanation: Put two runs side by side only when they trained on the same rows and differ in one deliberate parameter; then the metric difference belongs to that parameter. Notice in the first state that C = 1 and C = 0.01 share digest 4950f73b and differ only in C. In the second, the leaky run differs only in features, so the jump to 1.0 is the leak alone. In the third, the random split changes the rows and three parameters: [[dbxfe-mlflow-comparable-concept|comparable]] is a property of two records, not of two scores.

samajh.text: Do students ke marks tabhi compare karo jab paper, time aur checker teeno same hon. Agar ek ko aasaan paper mila aur doosre ko extra time bhi, toh marks ka farak kiski wajah se hai, koi nahi bata sakta. Ek hi cheez badlo, jaise sirf padhne ka tareeka, tab farak ka matlab banta hai.
samajh.mapping: The paper is the training rows (the digest), the time and checker are the other parameters, and changing only the study method is changing one parameter such as C.
samajh.boundary: Exam scores carry human variation; two runs on the same rows with a fixed seed can be repeated exactly, so a difference between them is not luck.

handbook.markdown:
Comparability can be decided from the records alone, before looking at a metric:

```python
def comparable(run_a, run_b):
    a, b = mlflow.get_run(run_a).data.params, mlflow.get_run(run_b).data.params
    differing = sorted(k for k in set(a) | set(b) if a.get(k) != b.get(k))
    same_rows = training_digest(run_a) is not None and training_digest(run_a) == training_digest(run_b)
    return {"differing_params": differing, "same_dataset_digest": same_rows,
            "comparable": same_rows and len(differing) == 1}
```

Run against the lab's experiment:

| pair | differing parameters | same rows | comparable |
|---|---|---|---|
| C-1 / C-0.01 | C | yes | yes |
| C-1 / leaky | features | yes | yes |
| C-1 / random split | split, train_fraction, train_through_day | no | no |
| C-1 / hero | eight | hero logged none | no |

Hold everything else fixed as well: the evaluation rows (the lab logs them with context `evaluation`), the library versions (logged as a parameter) and the metric definitions. Two runs evaluated on different test rows are not comparable even with identical training data.

`mlflow.search_runs()` makes the candidates easy to pull, for example `filter_string="params.split = 'time'"` with `order_by=["metrics.recall DESC"]`; the filter narrows by the record, and the comparability test above decides which pairs to read. When a pair is not comparable, the honest statement is "these differ in several ways at once", not a conclusion about any one of them.

Choosing between C = 1 and C = 0.01 on days 85 to 120 spends those days: whichever wins, its score there is a selection result, and the promotion beat says what confirms it. A comparable pair is not a validated pair. C-1 against the leaky run is a perfectly controlled comparison, and its lesson is that the leak inflates accuracy; the leaky run still fails the evidence gate later.

beats.recap: Same rows and one changed parameter: only then does a difference have one cause.

beats.title: The top of an accuracy-sorted table is where leaks live
beats.outcome: Read a sorted experiment table against its baselines and the measures that match the decision.
beats.explanation: Sorting runs by accuracy is the first thing a hurried reader does. Notice the order in the first state: the two runs that read the repair record tie at 1.0, and never-warn comes third at 0.9375 because only 18 of 288 test rows are faults. The model worth keeping is sixth. Read the same runs against the contract's measures and the table changes shape. Logging [[dbxfe-mlflow-baseline-concept|baselines]] as runs is what puts the rule in use and never-warn in the same table.

handbook.markdown:
The accuracy table is not wrong; it is answering a question nobody asked. With 18 faults in 288 test rows, the base rate alone gives 0.9375, and any column that encodes the label (repair_minutes is non-zero exactly on fault rows) gives 1.0. The top of a sorted table therefore collects two kinds of run: the ones that exploit class balance and the ones that exploit leakage.

The lab builds the table the way a reviewer would:

```python
frame = mlflow.search_runs(experiment_ids=[exp], order_by=["metrics.accuracy DESC"])
# columns: run_id, tags.mlflow.runName, params.C, params.split, metrics.accuracy, metrics.recall, ...
```

Then it re-reads the same rows through the contract. Recall is the share of the 18 faults caught; precision is the share of warnings that were real; warnings a day is warnings divided by the 36 test days, because the inspection round holds two ovens a day. The temperature rule catches 12 of 18 with 43 warnings (1.19 a day); the C = 1 model catches 15 of 18 with 68 warnings (1.89 a day). That comparison, model against the rule in use at a workable load, is the one the model evaluation report asks for.

Three habits make the table honest. Log the baselines as runs, with the same evaluation dataset, so they appear in every query. Log counts beside rates, so a reader sees that recall 0.8333 is 15 of 18. Sort by the decision's measure, and when a run tops the table by a wide margin, read its record before celebrating: in this experiment both perfect scores fail the evidence gate before their metrics are consulted.

Nothing here requires a better model. It requires reading the numbers in the currency of the decision, and a small test set (18 faults) is a reason to report the counts, not just the rates.

beats.recap: On rare faults, accuracy ranks never-warn and the leaks first; read the contract's measures instead.

beats.title: The best-looking run may be one nobody can rerun
beats.outcome: Compare a superior-looking run's record with a clean run's and name what blocks its reproduction.
beats.explanation: The hero run scored 1.0 on everything. Notice in the first state what its record holds: one parameter, model=logistic_regression, and nothing else a rerun needs. The reproduction step refuses and names eight gaps. In the second state the same code ran again: the record is identical and the result is not, 20 of 20 faults in one hidden test set, 18 of 18 in the other. When identical records hold different results, the number belongs to something unrecorded, so it cannot be [[dbxfe-mlflow-reproduce-concept|reproduced]].

samajh.text: Mummy ne ek din kaha, namak thoda sa, andaaz se. Us din sabzi kamaal ki bani, par kisi ne nahi likha kitna namak gaya, kaunsa masala, kitni der aanch. Agli baar wahi haath, wahi bartan, par swaad alag. Aur koi bata nahi sakta kyun, kyunki jo cheez badli woh kabhi likhi hi nahi gayi thi.
samajh.mapping: The unmeasured pinch of salt is the unlogged seed and split; the masala brand is the dataset and library version; a written recipe with exact amounts is a run record that can be rerun.
samajh.boundary: Cooking always varies a little; a seeded computation on the same machine and versions can repeat bit for bit, so any difference there points to something unrecorded.

handbook.markdown:
The hero is a composite of ordinary habits: a notebook that logs the model and a score, a random split with no seed, a feature list built interactively, and a model saved without a signature. The lab reproduces it on purpose:

```python
features = FEATURES + ["repair_minutes"]           # a post-event column
train, test = split_random(frame, 0.7, seed=None)  # a new permutation every execution
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="hero"):
    mlflow.log_param("model", "logistic_regression")
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model")   # no signature, no input example
    mlflow.log_metrics(metrics, model_id=info.model_id)
```

(The tests pass hidden seeds 11 and 12 so that the executions are checkable; the record still omits them.)

A reproduction step reads the record and refuses rather than guesses:

```text
cannot reproduce this run: not recorded: C, class_weight, features, max_iter,
scikit_learn, seed, split, training_dataset
```

Guessing would be worse than refusing. Trying seeds until the 1.0 comes back reproduces nothing: it searches for a test set that agrees with the claim.

Where hidden state comes from: unseeded splits and samplers, estimators whose `random_state` is left to chance, notebook cells executed out of order, a data extract that has since been overwritten, and library upgrades. Scikit-learn's guidance is to control randomness through `random_state`, passing an integer to splitters for repeatable splits. The record should hold every value the code reads, the training dataset, the feature list and the library versions; the next beat shows what a rerun does with them.

The hero is not rejected for its score. It is rejected because nobody, including its author, can say which rows produced the score or which columns the model read.

beats.recap: Identical records with different results: the number lives outside the record.

beats.title: A reproduction repeats the digest and every metric
beats.outcome: Decide whether a rerun is a reproduction, a new experiment or a refusal.
beats.explanation: Reproduction here has a strict meaning: rerun from the record alone, then compare. Notice the equation: the rerun must see the same training digest, run on the recorded library version, and return every metric equal. The clean C = 1 rerun meets all three, bit for bit. The same rerun on another plant's rows changes the digest and recall falls to 0.6: a new experiment, not a failed reproduction. A record claiming scikit-learn 1.8.0 on a 1.9.1 installation is refused before training.

handbook.markdown:
The lab's `reproduce()` reads only the record:

```python
run = mlflow.get_run(run_id)
params = run.data.params
missing = [k for k in ("model", "C", "class_weight", "max_iter", "seed", "split", "features")
           if k not in params]
if params.get("scikit_learn") != sklearn.__version__:
    raise ReproductionRefused(missing, ["scikit-learn ... recorded, ... installed"])
rerun = train_time_split(frame, C=float(params["C"]), seed=int(params["seed"]),
                         train_through_day=int(params["train_through_day"]),
                         features=params["features"].split(","), ...)
reproduced = same_digest and not differences      # every metric compared with ==
```

On the lab machine the rerun of time-split-C-1 returned digest 4950f73b and metrics equal to the original's with exact float equality. That is achievable because every source of variation was pinned: the rows (digest), the split (a day cut-off), the estimator (lbfgs with fixed data is deterministic), the library versions and the machine.

Three outcomes, three words:

- **Reproduced**: same digest, same environment, identical metrics.
- **New experiment**: the digest changed. Report both results; neither refutes the other.
- **Refused**: something needed is not recorded, or the environment differs. Name what, and do not run.

What can break exactness even with a complete record: a different CPU or linear-algebra (BLAS) library build, multi-threaded or GPU arithmetic, a library upgrade, or data re-extracted from a table that has changed since. For such cases decide in advance what tolerance counts as a reproduction and write it down with the contract; deciding after seeing the numbers turns a check into a negotiation. Also record the code version, for example a commit hash as a tag, because the record cannot rerun code that no longer exists.

beats.recap: Same digest, same versions, identical metrics: reproduced; new rows: a new experiment.

beats.title: A logged model is a directory that names its flavors
beats.outcome: Read an MLmodel file and choose how a consumer should load the model.
beats.explanation: `log_model` writes a directory whose MLmodel file lists [[dbxfe-mlflow-flavor-concept|flavors]]: python_function, the generic interface MLflow's tools load, and sklearn, the library's own. Notice the nodes: model.skops holds the fitted pipeline (skops was the default format for scikit-learn in MLflow 3.16.1), the environment files sit beside it, and in MLflow 3 the model is its own logged-model entity with an ID. In the second state, loading through python_function enforces the signature; the native flavor does not.

handbook.markdown:
The MLmodel file the lab's clean run wrote (abridged):

```yaml
flavors:
  python_function:
    env: {conda: conda.yaml, virtualenv: python_env.yaml}
    loader_module: mlflow.sklearn
    model_path: model.skops
    python_version: 3.12.3
  sklearn:
    pickled_model: model.skops
    serialization_format: skops
    sklearn_version: 1.9.1
mlflow_version: 3.16.1
model_id: m-<id>
run_id: <run id>
signature:
  inputs: '[{"type": "double", "name": "oven_age_years", "required": true}, ...]'
  outputs: '[{"type": "long", "name": "fault_next_24h", "required": true}]'
```

A flavor is a convention for loading. `python_function` is the one every MLflow Python model is expected to support and the one deployment tools use: `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri).predict(frame)` works the same for scikit-learn, XGBoost or custom code, and it is where signature enforcement happens. The `sklearn` flavor returns the fitted `Pipeline`, useful for inspecting coefficients, with no enforcement.

Serialization is a flavor detail with consequences. In the lab's MLflow 3.16.1 the scikit-learn flavor saved `model.skops` by default, which is why `skops` appears in the pinned requirements; pickle-based formats remain available but deserializing a pickle from an untrusted source can run code.

MLflow 3 changes how models are referenced: `log_model(model, name="model")` creates a LoggedModel with an ID, `models:/m-<id>` loads it before any registration, and metrics logged with `model_id=` attach to it. Older code and articles use `artifact_path=` and `runs:/<run_id>/model`; check the major version a project pins.

What to check before loading someone else's model: the flavors present, the serialization format, the signature, and the environment files, which the next beats cover.

beats.recap: MLmodel lists how to load a model; only python_function applies the signature.

beats.title: The signature is checked at the pyfunc door
beats.outcome: Predict which input changes schema enforcement rejects and which a contract must catch itself.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-mlflow-signature-concept|signature]] lists the model's inputs and outputs: here six required double columns and fault_next_24h as a long. When the model is loaded as python_function, MLflow checks each request before the model runs. Notice the second state: a renamed column and an int64 column are refused, a reordered frame passes because columns match by name, and an extra column is ignored with a warning. The third state logs a candidate from each drifted frame and checks its signature against a [[dbxfe-mlflow-contract-concept|model contract]]: every change is named, the extra column included. That check gates promotion; it never sees a request.

handbook.markdown:
The lab infers the signature from the model's real inputs and a named output:

```python
X_train = train[FEATURES].astype("float64")          # the model's inputs, as served
signature = infer_signature(X_train, pd.Series(model.predict(X_train.head(5)),
                                               name="fault_next_24h"))
mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model", signature=signature, input_example=X_train.head(3))
```

Casting to float64 first is deliberate: integer columns cannot hold missing values, and MLflow warns that an integer schema will reject a request whose integers arrive as floats because a value is missing. Naming the output gives `fault_next_24h: long` instead of an anonymous int64 tensor.

The documented enforcement rules are that missing required inputs raise and only lossless conversions are made; the lab observed what that means in 3.16.1: int32 is widened to double, int64 is refused, a string is refused, a reordered frame is accepted, and an extra column is dropped with the log line "These inputs will be ignored".

That last behaviour is why a contract checks the signature itself:

```python
expected = {c["name"]: c["type"] for c in contract["input_schema"]}
actual = {c["name"]: c["type"] for c in json.loads(signature["inputs"])}
reasons = ([f"missing_input:{n}" for n in sorted(set(expected) - set(actual))]
           + [f"unexpected_input:{n}" for n in sorted(set(actual) - set(expected))]
           + [f"type_mismatch:{n}:{expected[n]}->{actual[n]}"
              for n in sorted(set(expected) & set(actual)) if expected[n] != actual[n]])
```

The contract is versioned (1.0.0) so that a legitimate change, such as the plant renaming a sensor, becomes a new contract version and a retrained model, never a silent mapping. This check reads a logged model's signature, so it gates promotion: a candidate trained on a frame that carried `repair_minutes` is refused. It never sees a serving request, and a correctly signed model still drops an extra request column with only a warning. If such a request should fail loudly, check the request itself before `predict` (illustrative, not in the lab):

```python
def check_request(frame, contract):
    expected = {c["name"] for c in contract["input_schema"]}
    unexpected, missing = sorted(set(frame.columns) - expected), sorted(expected - set(frame.columns))
    if unexpected or missing:
        raise ValueError(f"request refused: unexpected={unexpected} missing={missing}")
```

MLflow already refuses missing inputs and unsafe types, so names are the gap it leaves.

beats.recap: MLflow refuses missing and unsafe inputs but ignores extras; the contract refuses an extra in a candidate's signature at promotion, and only a request check refuses it in a request.

beats.title: The environment travels with the model
beats.outcome: Read the environment files a logged model carries and decide when a version difference voids a reproduction.
beats.explanation: Logging the model also wrote requirements.txt, python_env.yaml and conda.yaml. Notice the pins in the first state: MLflow inferred mlflow 3.16.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas, numpy, scipy and skops from what the model imports, and python_env.yaml records Python 3.12.3. That [[dbxfe-mlflow-environment-concept|environment]] is part of the result. The second state shows the lab's reproduction step comparing the recorded scikit-learn version with the installed one and refusing a mismatch rather than calling a different computation the same.

handbook.markdown:
What the lab's model directory holds:

```text
requirements.txt   mlflow==3.16.1  numpy==2.5.3  pandas==3.0.6  scikit-learn==1.9.1  scipy==1.18.1  skops==0.15.0
python_env.yaml    python: 3.12.3; build_dependencies: pip, setuptools, wheel; dependencies: -r requirements.txt
conda.yaml         channels: conda-forge; python=3.12.3; pip: the same pins
```

MLflow infers these by loading the model in a subprocess and recording the packages it imports, then pinning the versions installed at logging time. The lab's test compares them with the lab's own `requirements.txt`: they match exactly. Edits to these files are overwritten the next time the model is saved; `extra_pip_requirements=` adds what inference misses, such as a package imported only inside custom code. Newer MLflow versions can also lock transitive dependencies.

Two environments are easy to confuse. The model's files describe what is needed to load and run the model. The training environment (the code that split, trained and evaluated) is not captured unless you record it: the lab logs `scikit_learn` as a run parameter, and a project should also tag the code version.

A reproduction step checks the recorded version before doing anything:

```python
if params["scikit_learn"] != sklearn.__version__:
    raise ReproductionRefused([], [f"scikit-learn {params['scikit_learn']} recorded, "
                                   f"{sklearn.__version__} installed"])
```

Refusing is conservative on purpose: a patch release may give identical numbers, but that is a claim to test, not assume. When a serving or scoring platform cannot install the model's pins, the options are to build its image from the model's files or to retrain there as a new run and a new version, with its own evidence.

beats.recap: The model carries its pins; a rerun on other versions is refused, not assumed equal.

beats.title: Versions stay fixed; the alias is the pointer you move
beats.outcome: Trace a model from run to logged model to registered version, and move an alias forward and back.
beats.explanation: Registering a logged model creates a numbered [[dbxfe-mlflow-version-concept|version]] of a registered model, with lineage to its run. An [[dbxfe-mlflow-alias-concept|alias]] such as candidate names one version and is loaded as models:/cinderline-oven-fault@candidate. Notice across the states: version 1 gets the alias, the reproduced rerun becomes version 2 and the alias moves, and moving it back is the rollback. No version changed, and versions 1 and 2 predict identically: a version records a registration, not unique content.

samajh.text: Hospital ki reception pe ek board hai: aaj ke duty doctor, Dr. Mehta. Doctors ki list waisi hi rehti hai, har doctor ka apna number hai. Kal Dr. Rao ki duty hai toh sirf board ka naam badalta hai, koi doctor hataya nahi jaata. Galat naam lag gaya toh board pe wapas Dr. Mehta likh do. Mareez sirf board padhkar jaate hain.
samajh.mapping: The doctors with fixed numbers are model versions, the board is the alias candidate, changing the board is promotion, restoring the old name is rollback, and patients reading the board are consumers loading by alias.
samajh.boundary: An alias points to exactly one version of one registered model, and moving it serves nothing by itself; a serving or batch system must read it.

handbook.markdown:
The registry calls the lab makes, all against the same temporary file store:

```python
client = MlflowClient()
version = mlflow.register_model(info.model_uri, "cinderline-oven-fault")   # version 1
client.set_model_version_tag("cinderline-oven-fault", version.version, "contract_version", "1.0.0")
client.set_model_version_tag("cinderline-oven-fault", version.version, "decided_from_run", run_id)
client.set_registered_model_alias("cinderline-oven-fault", "candidate", version.version)
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/cinderline-oven-fault@candidate")
```

Observed states: after the first registration the alias points to version 1; registering the reproduced rerun creates version 2 and moving the alias leaves version 1 with an empty alias list; moving it back restores version 1. `get_model_version_by_alias()` answers "which version is the candidate now?" and each version keeps its `run_id`, which is the lineage back to parameters, datasets and checks.

Why aliases rather than stages: an alias is an explicit, named pointer, a version can carry several (candidate and champion, say), and consumers that load by alias need no code change when the pointer moves. Stages still exist in the open-source registry but are not supported for models in Unity Catalog, where aliases and tags do this job.

Registering is not deploying. Nothing runs because an alias moved; a serving or batch system must read the alias. Keep evidence on the version itself (the contract version, the deciding run, a link to the decision file) so that a reader of the registry can get from the pointer back to the reasons.

A version is a registration event: the same model registered twice gets two numbers. Do not re-register to "update" a version, and do not delete old versions that an alias might need to return to.

beats.recap: Register once per decision, tag the evidence, and move the alias; a version's model never changes.

beats.title: Promotion reads the evidence before the metrics
beats.outcome: Apply a contract's evidence gate and thresholds and write the decision with its reasons.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-mlflow-promotion-concept|promotion decision]] applies a written, versioned contract in two gates. The evidence gate asks whether the record can be trusted: a time split, a seed, a training dataset, a feature list without post-event columns, a signature matching the contract. Only then are thresholds read. Notice in the first two states that three runs with attractive numbers stop at the first gate, C = 0.01 stops at the second, and C = 1 alone becomes a candidate. The third applies the same contract to another plant and rejects it.

handbook.markdown:
The contract is a file with a version, written before any run is judged:

```json
{"contract_version": "1.0.0", "model_name": "cinderline-oven-fault",
 "input_schema": [{"name": "oven_age_years", "type": "double"}, "... six in all"],
 "output": {"name": "fault_next_24h", "type": "long", "values": [0, 1]},
 "thresholds": {"recall_min": 0.75, "precision_min": 0.2, "warnings_per_day_max": 2.0},
 "evidence": {"split": "time", "post_event_features": "none", "seed_recorded": true,
              "dataset_digest_recorded": true, "signature_required": true}}
```

The thresholds come from the decision, not from the results: catch at least three faults in four, keep one warning in five real, and never add more ovens than the round of two can inspect. The recall floor also sits above the temperature rule's 0.6667, so a candidate must beat the rule in use.

```python
def decide(contract, run_id):
    evidence = evidence_report(contract, run_id)        # reads params, inputs and the model only
    if not evidence["ok"]:
        return {"decision": "reject", "gate": "evidence", "reasons": evidence["reasons"]}
    thresholds = threshold_report(contract, mlflow.get_run(run_id).data.metrics)
    return {"decision": "promote-candidate" if thresholds["ok"] else "reject",
            "gate": "thresholds", "reasons": thresholds["reasons"]}
```

The decision file lists the contract version, the thresholds, the baselines and every run with its gate and sorted reasons, and says in words that promote-candidate registers a version and moves an alias, deploys nothing, and does not certify data quality.

Three limits. Days 85 to 120 did two jobs here: they chose C = 1 over C = 0.01 and they produced the numbers the decision quotes, so they are a selection (validation) period, not an untouched test. Quote 0.8333 and 0.2206 as the selection result, and confirm the frozen candidate on a later period, such as the next month's oven-days, before calling them an estimate. The gate reads what a record declares, so a record that misstates its split would pass; the check reports stored as artifacts let a reviewer compare the declaration with the rows. And a passing decision belongs to one dataset and one period: the transfer plant's run shows the same code and contract rejecting on recall. The model evaluation report's decision section is where this entry belongs.

beats.recap: Evidence gate first, thresholds second, every reason written down; promotion deploys nothing.

beats.title: Databricks hosts the record; the evidence is still yours
beats.outcome: Separate the duties open-source MLflow leaves to you from those Databricks-managed MLflow and Unity Catalog take on.
beats.explanation: With open-source MLflow you choose, run and secure the tracking server, its stores and the registry; in 3.16.1 the default tracking URI is a local SQLite file. Databricks-managed MLflow hosts tracking in the workspace with experiment permissions and registers models in [[dbxfe-mlflow-uc-concept|Unity Catalog]]: three-level names, catalog privileges, aliases and tags, no stages. Notice what stays selected in both states: the contract and the data checks. No platform decides which run earns an alias.

handbook.markdown:
What changes, as a schematic diff (nothing here was executed on Databricks; workspace type, region and entitlements must be confirmed first):

```python
# open-source, as in the lab
os.environ["MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE"] = "true"      # file store: maintenance mode, explicit opt-in
mlflow.set_tracking_uri(tmp_dir.as_uri())
mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "cinderline-oven-fault")

# Databricks-managed MLflow with Unity Catalog
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")            # the default with MLflow 3 on Databricks
mlflow.register_model(model_uri, "cinderline_ml.maintenance.oven_fault")
```

| duty | open-source MLflow | Databricks-managed |
|---|---|---|
| tracking server and stores | you run, secure and back up | hosted in the workspace |
| who can see runs | your server's access control | experiment permissions (CAN READ, CAN EDIT, CAN MANAGE) |
| registry | same backend, versions and aliases | Unity Catalog: catalog.schema.model, privileges, aliases and tags, no stages |
| create a registered model | whatever your server's access control allows | USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and CREATE MODEL on the schema |
| load a model | whatever your server's access control allows | EXECUTE on the model |
| which run earns an alias | the team | the team |
| was the data valid | the team | the team |

For self-hosted MLflow, current releases steer away from the file store: the default tracking URI in 3.16.1 is a SQLite file, and `mlflow migrate-filestore` moves an existing file store's metadata into SQLite while leaving artifacts where they are.

Ownership rules for versions and aliases in Unity Catalog are the detail most likely to change, so check the privileges reference before designing who may move a production alias. The alias itself behaves as in the lab: one pointer per name, moved on evidence, with versions fixed. Platform lineage and permissions make the record easier to trust as a record; they do not make a leaky feature valid.

beats.recap: The platform hosts and governs the record; the contract and the data checks stay with the team.

extensionCards.prompt: Why did the lab have to opt in to the ./mlruns-style file store, and what does MLflow document as the way out?
extensionCards.answer: MLflow 3.16.1 treats the file store as maintenance-mode and raises unless MLFLOW_ALLOW_FILE_STORE=true is set; mlflow migrate-filestore moves its metadata to SQLite.
extensionCards.explanation: The error the installed MLflow raises points to a database backend and to the [[dbxfe-mlflow-extension-filestore-concept|file store migration]]. The documented tool needs MLflow 3.10 or later, targets SQLite only (file-store experiment IDs exceed the 32-bit integers PostgreSQL and MySQL enforce), moves metadata losslessly, leaves artifacts in their original location with the database storing the same artifact URIs, and rolls back on error. The lab keeps the file store only because it lives in a temporary directory that is deleted.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Most older tutorials default to ./mlruns; a team starting today should plan a database backend and know the migration path.

extensionCards.prompt: How does an MLflow 3 LoggedModel change the way you reference a model and read its metrics?
extensionCards.answer: A logged model has its own ID and URI, models:/<model_id>, can be logged outside a run, and metrics can be linked to it directly.
extensionCards.explanation: In MLflow 2 a model was an artifact path inside a run, referenced as runs:/<run_id>/model. The MLflow 3 [[dbxfe-mlflow-extension-logged-model-concept|LoggedModel]] is a first-class entity: log_model takes a name, returns a model ID, and metrics logged with model_id attach to the model, so a registry reader can see a version's metrics without opening the run. The lab used this: every clean run's evaluation metrics are linked to its logged model.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Code and articles written for MLflow 2 use artifact_path and runs:/ URIs; mixing the two styles is a common source of broken model references.

extensionCards.prompt: Which Unity Catalog privileges separate creating a registered model from loading one for inference?
extensionCards.answer: Creating needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA with CREATE MODEL on the schema; loading needs EXECUTE on the model.
extensionCards.explanation: The [[dbxfe-mlflow-extension-uc-privileges-concept|registered model privileges]] split duties cleanly: a training principal can create the model in a schema it may write to, while a scoring job needs only EXECUTE, which also allows reading version metadata and downloading model files. Creating further versions and setting aliases are tied to ownership of the registered model or to a privilege the reference names for that purpose, so who may move a production alias is a governance decision to check against the current privileges reference before granting.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Promotion by evidence only holds if the people who can move an alias are the ones who apply the contract.

extensionCards.prompt: Who can read or change the runs in a Databricks experiment, and how does a notebook experiment differ?
extensionCards.answer: Principals granted CAN READ, CAN EDIT or CAN MANAGE on a workspace experiment; a notebook experiment follows its notebook's permissions.
extensionCards.explanation: [[dbxfe-mlflow-extension-experiment-permissions-concept|Experiment permissions]] come in four levels: NO PERMISSIONS, CAN READ, CAN EDIT and CAN MANAGE. A workspace experiment is independent of any notebook, and any notebook can log to it by ID or name. A notebook experiment is tied to one notebook, created automatically when a run starts without an active experiment, and managed through that notebook. For a promotion review, put the runs in a workspace experiment whose readers are the reviewers.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Runs logged into an automatically created notebook experiment can be invisible to the reviewer who has to judge them.

recap.title: A number is only as good as its record
recap.markdown: **Every number a model report quotes should trace to a run that could be rerun.** A run records parameters, metrics, datasets, artifacts and a model; a digest says which rows, not whether they were right; two runs compare only when one thing changed; a reproduction repeats the digest and every metric, and a record that cannot be rerun is refused, however good its score. The model carries its flavors, signature and environment, a versioned contract names, at promotion, the drift MLflow lets through, and promotion reads the evidence before the metrics and moves an alias, nothing more. Databricks hosts and governs the record; the judgement stays yours. **Transfer challenge:** take a predictive-maintenance experiment from another industry, such as pump failures at a water utility, and write the contract's evidence clause, the comparable pairs and the decision entry for its best-scoring run before reading any metric.

appliedTask.title: Review the East plant's press-seal promotion request
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline's East plant predicts, at the start of each shift, whether each of its twelve hydraulic presses will lose a seal before the shift ends; maintenance can service two presses a shift. The experiment holds: P-1 with a time split, a seed, training digest 9d2e41c0, seven sensor features and a matching signature, recall 0.72 and 1.6 warnings a shift; P-2, identical except max_depth, recall 0.81 and 2.4 warnings a shift; P-3 with accuracy 0.99, split=random, no seed, no dataset and a signature with eight inputs including seal_replaced_at; and the pressure-threshold rule in use at recall 0.41. The contract asks recall of at least 0.7, precision of at least 0.25 and at most 2.0 warnings a shift. Write the decision entries, the registry actions and what the record cannot tell you.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: P-3: reject at the evidence gate with split_not_time_based, seed_not_recorded, dataset_digest_missing, features_not_recorded and unexpected_input:seal_replaced_at, a column written after the failure it predicts; its 0.99 is never read. P-1 and P-2 share digest 9d2e41c0 and differ only in max_depth, so they are comparable. P-2 is rejected at the thresholds gate with warnings_above_cap (2.4 against 2.0). P-1 meets recall (0.72) and the cap (1.6) and beats the rule's 0.41, but its precision must be read from its record against 0.25 before it can be decided. If it passes: register P-1 as a new version, tag it with the contract version and run ID, and move the alias candidate. The record cannot say whether the logged sensor data was valid, how P-1 behaves on presses absent from training, or anything about serving.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer applies the evidence gate before any metric, uses the shared digest and the single differing parameter to decide comparability, refuses to decide on a threshold the brief does not report, and states the limits a complete record still leaves open.
